title: Australia Regulates Supplements Like Drugs, but Nobody Checks Whether They Work
dek: Australia puts supplements and pharmaceuticals under the same agency, which looks strict; but efficacy is neither reviewed before market nor tested during production — the impression of "good" was planted by marketing and cross-border policy.
why: The first half's regulatory breakdown is solid, and the second half's chain from marketing to daigou policy is complete; but the middle section has a lot of transcription garble, and the information density is uneven.
who: Investors and founders looking at consumer brands, supplements and cross-border e-commerce, plus anyone doing brand marketing or interested in where regulatory arbitrage exists.

points.h: Australians treating themselves is a tradition
points.body: The soil for Australia's supplement industry isn't the natural environment, it's four social habits: a sparse population spread over a vast area, which pushed people to self-medicate; pharmacists who also diagnose and dispense; naturopathic industry organisations dating back to the 1920s; and health food stores resembling food-as-medicine shops. Stack those four together and Australians came to take "solving health problems without going to hospital" for granted. Black Moth (澳佳宝) started as a naturopathic clinic, and only after the second generation took over did it translate that into products the mainstream system could recognise — turning "take a spoonful of fish oil a day" into a standardised fish oil capsule, for instance.

points.h: The contract manufacturers are the industry's foundation
points.body: Pen Pharmaceuticals, which appeared in 1974, was Australia's first company focused on contract manufacturing for supplements, and by around 2003 it was producing roughly 70% of Australia's vitamins, minerals and herbal products. Its value lay in process know-how: tablets, compound ingredients, the rubber-and-oil seal on soft capsules, the mixing uniformity of powders, the stability of liquids — each is its own set of solutions. In the 1980s and 90s a new generation of contract manufacturers extended their services in both directions, moving from pure production (CMO) to CDMO covering formulation, ingredients, trial production, labelling, packaging, testing, and registration for export. The brand only has to hand over a concept, and the factory can turn it into a product ready to sell.

points.h: A registration system means nobody looks before market
points.body: Australia legislated in 1989, putting the TGA in charge of both pharmaceuticals and supplements, and all products must obtain an AUST number. Most supplements fall into the AUSTL category: they may only use low-risk ingredients permitted by the TGA and may only make low-level health claims, and companies can get a number just by applying themselves — the TGA does no pre-market review, only post-market spot checks. By around 2010 Australia had roughly ten thousand complementary medicines, of which nearly 98% sat in this registration system. Only prescription drugs, over-the-counter drugs and a small number of high-risk supplements enter the AUSTR tier, which is where the TGA must assess safety, quality and efficacy in advance.

points.h: It looks strict, but in practice it is loose
points.body: Put the contract manufacturing and regulatory lines together and you see that GMP only guarantees the factory produces consistently to the standard the brand gives it, and that problems can be traced back to a batch for recall — it is not itself responsible for whether the product works. The TGA side only handles declarations and issuing batch numbers; efficacy is explained by the brand itself. So the claim that "Australia regulates supplements like drugs" is not wrong in itself, but it is misleading: the method of regulation is the same, while the regulatory standard applied to the efficacy part differs enormously. The whole system exercises no effective upfront oversight of a product's actual effects, and there is a risk of disconnect between the brand and the product's efficacy.

points.h: The marketing was copied from Centrum, not invented
points.body: Radek Sali, who took over as CEO in 2008, did not conjure a marketing plan out of thin air. He did industry research and found the best seller among peers was Centrum, and the feedback from retailers was: Centrum didn't give the channel much margin, but you couldn't argue with it advertising heavily on TV all year round, with great athlete endorsements, so consumers would walk into a pharmacy and ask for it by name. Sali wanted to replicate that at Swisse. He started with Australia's national sport, cricket — the men's team captain, buying only very short ad slots during the hottest summer cricket broadcasts, so that even on a limited budget he could appear at important moments. But the female-dominated sales channel wasn't moved; some buyers didn't watch cricket themselves and didn't know the athlete. He asked his mother what shows she liked, and she said a dance variety show, and the strategy pivoted from there to spoken endorsements in entertainment content.

Swisse's bigger promotional push drew on Oprah and Ellen, and signed a three-year deal with the actress Nicole Kidman, extending its reach from Australia to the United States. By 2012 Swisse had 25 brand ambassadors, had shot more than 80 TV commercials in the previous 12 months, and reached annual revenue of A$183 million, with marketing spend of A$40-50 million a year — reportedly at one point the highest marketing spend of any consumer brand in Australia. Its ads didn't emphasise efficacy or ingredients; they mainly presented a state of being energetic, positively self-disciplined and good-looking — converting health into a lifestyle consumers aspire to. In 2012 Swisse took more than 20% market share in Australian supermarket channels and more than 10% in pharmacy channels.

points.h: The growth was found in Chinese pharmacies
points.body: Swisse spent heavily on the US market without much success, and on returning to its home market in Australia found that Swisse sold extremely well in pharmacies in Chinese-populated areas, with some stores selling at ten times the level of an ordinary store — because students and Chinese immigrants were buying it in bulk to take back to China or resell online, that is, daigou. Two policy shifts came in 2015: in March the Hangzhou cross-border e-commerce comprehensive pilot zone was approved, and in June China and Australia signed a free trade agreement, which formally took effect that December. The FTA mainly affected ordinary trade; Australian official statistics put the tariff on vitamins and supplements generally at 3% to 10%, while Black Moth itself estimated an average rate of 20%, and after the agreement it was said at the time that this could fall to zero within four years. Cross-border e-commerce ran through bonded warehouses, platforms bought in bulk, logistics time and cost fell sharply, and such goods were treated under the policy as for personal use, so they did not have to go through the registration and filing process for supplement imports.

points.h: The brand was bought; the impression stayed put
points.body: In September 2015 the Hong Kong-listed company Biostime completed the acquisition of a controlling stake in Swisse, and two years later completed a full buyout, a deal of about A$1.7 billion, or RMB 8.7 billion. For Swisse the deal carried little premium; for Biostime it added a large chunk of business revenue and imagination. All those Swisse ads in Hunan TV variety shows now are, in theory, a Chinese supplement company spending the money, yet the brand can still say it is an Australian supplement brand, and consumers can still apply their old, vague good impression of Australia to it — a large proportion of the acquisition's core value settles in the brand's goodwill.

A common international standard at the production level, ensuring consistent production to standard and traceable recalls, but not responsible for efficacy.

terms.def: A CMO takes on only the production step; a CDMO also takes in development work such as formulation, ingredients, trial production and registration filings.

quotes.text: The GMP system itself is not responsible for the product's efficacy; it can only prove that the contract manufacturer produced to the standard the brand gave it.
The whole system actually looks strict but is loose in practice, especially when it comes to the efficacy part.
This looseness means that no part of the system exercises any effective upfront oversight of the product's actual effects.
It doesn't emphasise efficacy or ingredients; it mainly presents a state of being energetic, positively self-disciplined and good-looking — it turns health into a lifestyle consumers aspire to.
The supplement industry has no particular barrier to entry; if everyone isn't competing on marketing, then for now no one has found the next thing to compete on.
When consumers face something they aren't familiar with, it's actually very easy for them to string together other familiar and trustworthy concepts to understand this unfamiliar thing.

We tend to remember some particularly simple concepts or judgments, so simple that you forget how many layers of logic lie behind them, so the more a business idea resembles common sense, the more it deserves the question: how did it come about, and how did it become so-called common sense?
